title: Physiology
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned 300L Biology general/animal physiology curriculum: homeostasis, membrane transport, nervous and muscle physiology, cardiovascular and respiratory physiology, digestive and renal physiology, endocrine control, blood, and thermoregulation.

questions.question: Homeostasis is best defined as:
options: The growth of an organism over time
The maintenance of a relatively stable internal environment despite external changes
The breakdown of food into usable energy
questions.correct_answer: The maintenance of a relatively stable internal environment despite external changes
questions.explanation: Homeostasis refers to the physiological processes that keep internal conditions such as temperature, pH, and osmolarity within a narrow, stable range.

questions.question: Most homeostatic control mechanisms in the body operate through:
options: Negative feedback loops that counteract deviations from a set point
questions.correct_answer: Negative feedback loops that counteract deviations from a set point
questions.explanation: Negative feedback is the predominant homeostatic mechanism: a deviation from the set point triggers a response that opposes and corrects the deviation, restoring balance.

questions.question: Childbirth (labour contractions stimulated by oxytocin) is a classic physiological example of:
questions.correct_answer: Positive feedback
questions.explanation: During labour, uterine contractions stimulate oxytocin release, which increases contractions further, escalating the response until birth occurs, an example of positive feedback.

questions.question: The movement of water across a semipermeable membrane from a region of lower solute concentration to higher solute concentration is called:
questions.correct_answer: Osmosis
questions.explanation: Osmosis is the passive diffusion of water molecules across a semipermeable membrane toward the side with higher solute concentration (lower water potential).

questions.question: Active transport across a cell membrane differs from facilitated diffusion in that active transport:
options: Moves substances against their concentration gradient and requires energy (ATP)
Always moves substances down their concentration gradient
questions.correct_answer: Moves substances against their concentration gradient and requires energy (ATP)
questions.explanation: Active transport uses cellular energy, typically from ATP hydrolysis, to move solutes against their concentration gradient, unlike passive facilitated diffusion.

questions.question: The sodium-potassium (Na+/K+) pump moves ions across the cell membrane in which pattern per cycle?
options: Equal numbers of Na+ and K+ in both directions
questions.correct_answer: 3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in
questions.explanation: The Na+/K+-ATPase pumps three sodium ions out of the cell and two potassium ions into the cell per ATP hydrolysed, maintaining the resting membrane potential.

questions.question: The resting membrane potential of a typical neuron is approximately:
questions.correct_answer: -70 mV
questions.explanation: A typical neuron at rest has an inside membrane potential of about -70 mV relative to the outside, mainly due to K+ permeability and the Na+/K+ pump.

questions.question: During the rising (depolarisation) phase of an action potential, the membrane potential changes mainly because:
options: Voltage-gated sodium channels open, allowing Na+ to rush into the cell
Voltage-gated potassium channels open, allowing K+ to rush out
questions.correct_answer: Voltage-gated sodium channels open, allowing Na+ to rush into the cell
questions.explanation: Depolarisation occurs when voltage-gated Na+ channels open in response to a threshold stimulus, causing a rapid influx of Na+ that makes the inside of the membrane more positive.

questions.question: At a chemical synapse, an arriving action potential triggers neurotransmitter release from the presynaptic terminal mainly through influx of which ion?
questions.correct_answer: Calcium (Ca2+)
questions.explanation: Depolarisation of the presynaptic terminal opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channels; the resulting Ca2+ influx triggers synaptic vesicles to fuse with the membrane and release neurotransmitter.

questions.question: Acetylcholine acting at the neuromuscular junction on skeletal muscle fibres binds to receptors on the motor end plate, causing:
options: Hyperpolarisation and inhibition of muscle contraction
Depolarisation that can trigger an action potential and muscle contraction
Direct contraction without any electrical change
questions.correct_answer: Depolarisation that can trigger an action potential and muscle contraction
questions.explanation: Acetylcholine binds nicotinic receptors on the motor end plate, opening ligand-gated cation channels that depolarise the muscle fibre and, if threshold is reached, trigger contraction.

questions.question: According to the sliding filament theory of muscle contraction, shortening of the sarcomere occurs because:
options: Actin and myosin filaments themselves shorten in length
Myosin heads pull thin actin filaments over thick myosin filaments, without either filament changing length
Calcium ions physically shorten the filaments
questions.correct_answer: Myosin heads pull thin actin filaments over thick myosin filaments, without either filament changing length
questions.explanation: In the sliding filament model, myosin cross-bridges repeatedly attach, pull, and release actin filaments, sliding them past the myosin filaments and shortening the sarcomere, while filament lengths remain unchanged.

questions.question: In skeletal muscle contraction, calcium ions released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum trigger contraction by binding to:
options: Troponin, causing tropomyosin to shift and expose myosin-binding sites on actin
Actin directly, forming a permanent bond
questions.correct_answer: Troponin, causing tropomyosin to shift and expose myosin-binding sites on actin
questions.explanation: Calcium binds troponin, causing a conformational change that moves tropomyosin away from myosin-binding sites on actin, allowing cross-bridge cycling to proceed.

questions.question: Cardiac muscle differs from skeletal muscle in that cardiac muscle cells are connected by:
options: Intercalated discs containing gap junctions that allow direct electrical coupling between cells
questions.correct_answer: Intercalated discs containing gap junctions that allow direct electrical coupling between cells
questions.explanation: Intercalated discs contain gap junctions that electrically couple cardiac muscle cells, allowing the heart to function as a coordinated syncytium.

questions.question: The sinoatrial (SA) node is often called the 'natural pacemaker' of the heart because it:
options: Is the only part of the heart capable of contracting
Generates spontaneous electrical impulses at the fastest rate, setting the heart's rhythm
Pumps blood directly to the lungs
questions.correct_answer: Generates spontaneous electrical impulses at the fastest rate, setting the heart's rhythm
questions.explanation: The SA node, located in the right atrium, spontaneously depolarises faster than other cardiac tissue, initiating and setting the pace for each heartbeat.

questions.question: During the cardiac cycle, the 'lub' sound of the heartbeat is produced mainly by:
options: Closure of the atrioventricular (mitral and tricuspid) valves at the start of ventricular systole
Closure of the semilunar (aortic and pulmonary) valves at the start of diastole
questions.correct_answer: Closure of the atrioventricular (mitral and tricuspid) valves at the start of ventricular systole
questions.explanation: The first heart sound ('lub') results from closure of the atrioventricular valves as the ventricles begin to contract, preventing backflow into the atria.

questions.question: Blood pressure is typically expressed as systolic over diastolic pressure; the diastolic value represents:
options: The pressure in the arteries when the ventricles contract
The pressure in the arteries when the ventricles are relaxed and filling
The pressure inside the atria only
The pressure in the pulmonary veins
questions.correct_answer: The pressure in the arteries when the ventricles are relaxed and filling
questions.explanation: Diastolic pressure is the lower arterial pressure recorded during ventricular relaxation (diastole), between heartbeats.

questions.question: Which blood vessels are responsible for the actual exchange of gases, nutrients, and wastes between blood and tissues?
questions.correct_answer: Capillaries
questions.explanation: Capillaries have thin, single-cell-layer walls that permit diffusion of gases, nutrients, and metabolic wastes between the blood and surrounding tissues.

questions.question: Haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen decreases in tissues with high carbon dioxide, low pH, and high temperature; this relationship is known as the:
questions.correct_answer: Bohr effect
questions.explanation: The Bohr effect describes how increased CO2, decreased pH (increased H+), and higher temperature reduce haemoglobin's oxygen affinity, promoting oxygen release to metabolically active tissues.

questions.question: During inspiration (inhalation), the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles contract, which:
options: Decreases thoracic cavity volume and increases intrapulmonary pressure
Increases thoracic cavity volume, decreasing intrapulmonary pressure below atmospheric pressure so air flows in
Has no effect on lung volume
Directly pumps air into the alveoli using muscular force
questions.correct_answer: Increases thoracic cavity volume, decreasing intrapulmonary pressure below atmospheric pressure so air flows in
questions.explanation: Contraction of the diaphragm and external intercostals expands the thoracic cavity, lowering intrapulmonary pressure below atmospheric pressure so air flows into the lungs (Boyle's law).

questions.question: The majority of carbon dioxide is transported in the blood in the form of:
options: Bicarbonate ions (HCO3-) after conversion by carbonic anhydrase
questions.correct_answer: Bicarbonate ions (HCO3-) after conversion by carbonic anhydrase
questions.explanation: Roughly 70% of CO2 is transported as bicarbonate ions, formed when CO2 combines with water in red blood cells via carbonic anhydrase, dissociating into HCO3- and H+.

questions.question: Tidal volume in human respiration refers to:
options: The maximum volume of air that can be forcibly exhaled after maximum inhalation
The volume of air inhaled or exhaled in a single normal, resting breath
The volume of air remaining in the lungs after maximal exhalation
questions.correct_answer: The volume of air inhaled or exhaled in a single normal, resting breath
questions.explanation: Tidal volume is the amount of air moved into or out of the lungs during a single normal breath at rest, typically about 500 mL in adult humans.

questions.question: Salivary amylase, secreted in the mouth, begins the digestion of:
questions.correct_answer: Starch (carbohydrates)
questions.explanation: Salivary amylase (ptyalin) hydrolyses starch into smaller polysaccharides and maltose, beginning carbohydrate digestion in the mouth.

questions.question: Pepsin, the main protein-digesting enzyme of the stomach, functions optimally in the:
options: Strongly alkaline environment of the stomach
Strongly acidic environment created by hydrochloric acid secreted by parietal cells
Neutral pH environment of the small intestine
Basic environment produced by bile salts
questions.correct_answer: Strongly acidic environment created by hydrochloric acid secreted by parietal cells
questions.explanation: Parietal cells secrete HCl, creating the highly acidic gastric environment (pH around 1.5-3.5) in which pepsin is activated from pepsinogen and functions optimally.

questions.question: Bile, produced by the liver and stored in the gallbladder, aids digestion primarily by:
options: Chemically breaking down proteins into amino acids
Emulsifying fats into smaller droplets, increasing the surface area for lipase action
Neutralising stomach acid before it reaches the mouth
questions.correct_answer: Emulsifying fats into smaller droplets, increasing the surface area for lipase action
questions.explanation: Bile salts emulsify large fat globules into smaller droplets, greatly increasing the surface area available for pancreatic lipase to hydrolyse triglycerides.

questions.question: Most nutrient absorption in the digestive tract occurs in the:
options: Small intestine, aided by villi and microvilli that increase surface area
questions.correct_answer: Small intestine, aided by villi and microvilli that increase surface area
questions.explanation: The small intestine is the primary site of nutrient absorption, its villi and microvilli greatly increasing surface area for efficient uptake of digested nutrients.

questions.question: The functional unit of the kidney, responsible for filtration and urine formation, is the:
questions.correct_answer: Nephron
questions.explanation: The nephron is the structural and functional unit of the kidney, consisting of the glomerulus, Bowman's capsule, and a system of tubules that filter blood and form urine.

questions.question: Glomerular filtration in the nephron is driven mainly by:
options: Hydrostatic (blood) pressure forcing fluid out of the glomerular capillaries into Bowman's capsule
Osmotic pressure pulling water into the capillaries
Muscular contraction of the nephron tubules
questions.correct_answer: Hydrostatic (blood) pressure forcing fluid out of the glomerular capillaries into Bowman's capsule
questions.explanation: Glomerular filtration is a passive process driven largely by blood hydrostatic pressure, which forces water and small solutes out of glomerular capillaries into Bowman's capsule.

questions.question: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH/vasopressin) regulates water balance by acting on the kidney to:
options: Decrease water reabsorption, producing more dilute urine
Increase permeability of the collecting duct to water, increasing water reabsorption and producing more concentrated urine
Stimulate secretion of glucose into the urine
questions.correct_answer: Increase permeability of the collecting duct to water, increasing water reabsorption and producing more concentrated urine
questions.explanation: ADH increases aquaporin insertion in the collecting duct cells, increasing water reabsorption back into the blood and reducing urine volume while concentrating it.

questions.question: A hormone is best defined as:
options: A chemical messenger secreted directly into a duct and delivered locally
A chemical messenger secreted into the bloodstream by an endocrine gland, which travels to and affects distant target cells
An enzyme that speeds up digestion only
A structural protein found in muscle
questions.correct_answer: A chemical messenger secreted into the bloodstream by an endocrine gland, which travels to and affects distant target cells
questions.explanation: Hormones are chemical signalling molecules released by endocrine glands directly into the blood, which then act on distant target cells bearing the appropriate receptors.

questions.question: Insulin, secreted by the beta cells of the pancreatic islets of Langerhans, lowers blood glucose mainly by:
options: Stimulating the liver to break down glycogen into glucose
Promoting uptake of glucose into cells (especially muscle and adipose tissue) and its conversion to glycogen for storage
Increasing glucose reabsorption in the kidney
questions.correct_answer: Promoting uptake of glucose into cells (especially muscle and adipose tissue) and its conversion to glycogen for storage
questions.explanation: Insulin lowers blood glucose by promoting cellular glucose uptake (via GLUT4 transporters) and stimulating glycogenesis, the conversion of glucose to glycogen for storage.

questions.question: Glucagon, secreted by pancreatic alpha cells, has the opposite effect to insulin by:
options: Raising blood glucose by stimulating glycogen breakdown (glycogenolysis) in the liver
questions.correct_answer: Raising blood glucose by stimulating glycogen breakdown (glycogenolysis) in the liver
questions.explanation: Glucagon raises blood glucose levels by stimulating the liver to break down stored glycogen into glucose and release it into the bloodstream, opposing insulin's action.

questions.question: Most endocrine hormone secretion is regulated by negative feedback involving the:
options: Hypothalamus and pituitary gland, which form a major regulatory axis for many endocrine glands
questions.correct_answer: Hypothalamus and pituitary gland, which form a major regulatory axis for many endocrine glands
questions.explanation: The hypothalamus-pituitary axis regulates many endocrine glands (thyroid, adrenal, gonads) through releasing hormones and negative feedback loops involving circulating hormone levels.

questions.question: Erythropoietin, produced mainly by the kidneys in response to low blood oxygen, stimulates:
options: White blood cell production in the spleen
Red blood cell production (erythropoiesis) in the bone marrow
questions.correct_answer: Red blood cell production (erythropoiesis) in the bone marrow
questions.explanation: Erythropoietin is released by the kidneys in response to hypoxia and stimulates the bone marrow to increase production of red blood cells.

questions.question: In the blood clotting cascade, the final common step involves the conversion of:
options: Fibrinogen into fibrin threads that form a mesh trapping blood cells
questions.correct_answer: Fibrinogen into fibrin threads that form a mesh trapping blood cells
questions.explanation: The clotting cascade converges on thrombin converting soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin strands, which form a mesh that stabilises the platelet plug into a clot.

questions.question: In humans, thermoregulation in response to high body temperature includes which mechanism?
options: Vasoconstriction of skin blood vessels and shivering
Vasodilation of skin blood vessels and increased sweating to promote heat loss
Contraction of arrector pili muscles to trap heat
questions.correct_answer: Vasodilation of skin blood vessels and increased sweating to promote heat loss
questions.explanation: When body temperature rises, the hypothalamus triggers vasodilation of skin blood vessels (increasing heat radiation) and sweating (heat loss through evaporation) to cool the body.

questions.question: The hypothalamus functions as the body's primary thermoregulatory centre by:
options: Directly producing heat through muscle contraction
Detecting blood temperature changes and coordinating autonomic responses such as sweating, shivering, and vasomotor changes
questions.correct_answer: Detecting blood temperature changes and coordinating autonomic responses such as sweating, shivering, and vasomotor changes
questions.explanation: The hypothalamus acts as the body's thermostat, sensing blood temperature and triggering appropriate effector responses (sweating, shivering, vasodilation/vasoconstriction) to maintain thermal homeostasis.
